                               byq$RMSE[4], byq$RMSE[1],
                               sqrt(mean(err[new_scaffold == FALSE, residual^2])),
                               sqrt(mean(err[new_scaffold == TRUE, residual^2]))),
  "known limitations" = sprintf("regresses to the mean at the extremes (%+.2f below pActivity 5.5, %+.2f above 7.5); the largest errors concentrate on single-measurement compounds and on activity cliffs",
                               mean(err[y < 5.5, residual]), mean(err[y > 7.5, residual])),
  "intended use"     = "ranking of analogues inside known ROCK1 chemotypes; NOT absolute potency prediction",
  "sanity checks"    = sprintf("shuffled-label R2 = %+.3f; no preprocessing fitted outside a fold", shuf[["R2"]]))
for (k in names(card)) cat(sprintf("%-29s: %s\n", k, card[[k]]))
## model                        : ranger(num.trees = 300, seed = 1) on frozen Morgan(r = 2, 2048 bit) fingerprints
## task                         : regression of pActivity (-log10 M) for ROCK1 (CHEMBL3231) inhibitors
## unit of prediction           : one standardised parent structure (InChIKey)
## training data                : 2211 compounds from the curated ChEMBL snapshot (exact measurements only)
## excluded                     : 1516 censored compounds (all measurements '>' or '<')
## split                        : random 80/20 by compound, set.seed(0); inner 5-fold CV for all comparisons
## test performance             : RMSE 0.738, MAE 0.575, R2 0.585, Spearman 0.774 on 553 held-out compounds
## baseline                     : predicting the training mean gives RMSE 1.099
## performance by applicability : RMSE 0.68 in the most-similar quartile vs 0.80 in the least-similar; 0.73 for known scaffolds vs 0.76 for unseen ones
## known limitations            : regresses to the mean at the extremes (-0.86 below pActivity 5.5, +0.73 above 7.5); the largest errors concentrate on single-measurement compounds and on activity cliffs
## intended use                 : ranking of analogues inside known ROCK1 chemotypes; NOT absolute potency prediction
## sanity checks                : shuffled-label R2 = -0.002; no preprocessing fitted outside a fold

Everything in the card is a number this document produced, and every entry answers a question a referee asks. The two entries that distinguish a careful card from a decorative one are “performance by applicability” — performance split by whether the compound resembles the training data — and “intended use”, which is where you write down the thing the model is not for. In a real project this list is written to model_card.md next to the serialised model (Unit 23 turns it into a Methods section, Unit 24 into a tested package).

Bridge — where this unit sits

The neighbouring units supply what this one simplified. Unit 12 (R) replaces the random split by the full split taxonomy and puts confidence intervals on every number above; Unit 13 (R) does feature selection properly, with stability across folds; Unit 14 (R) tunes the forest and its boosted cousins under a budget. The R-edition index lists the remaining units — Unit 9 explains the ridge baseline, Unit 17 turns “similarity below 0.6” into a calibrated applicability domain, Unit 23 turns the model card into a Methods section — and each has a Python counterpart under Material/; the Python version of this very unit is here. The algorithms themselves are the subject of the artificial-intelligence course, whose R edition covers model evaluation in S1 and trees and forests in U4; the chemistry of the representation is Unit 5 of the cheminformatics course and the curation behind the table is its Unit 7. For the structural side of ROCK1 see BGM324 Unit 3.

10. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • the seven decisions of a supervised project, and why only one is about the algorithm;
  • why the unit of prediction must be the entity you will be asked to predict (compound, not measurement; patient, not tissue site);
  • when a question is a regression, a classification at a stated threshold, or a ranking problem, with the metric for each;
  • what caret::train(preProcess = ...), a recipes recipe and a fit/transform closure guarantee, and which featurisation steps are safe outside them;
  • why a score is meaningless without a baseline, and which three baselines to compute;
  • how to read a learning curve and decide between more data and more capacity;
  • how to turn an error analysis into a statement about the applicability of the model;
  • the five leakage sources, the optimism each produces, and the checklist that catches them;
  • what belongs in a model card.

The single number to take away: on this dataset, selecting 50 of 2,048 features outside the cross-validation inflates \(R^2\) by 0.240 at n = 150 and by 0.010 at n = 2,764 — and on pure noise it manufactures an \(R^2\) of +0.563 out of nothing.

11. Self-assessment

  1. A colleague reports an \(R^2\) of 0.72 for a QSAR model. What are the first three questions you ask?
Computed on what — cross-validation or a held-out set, under which split? Against which baseline? And what is the unit of prediction, compounds or measurements? Without those three the number is not interpretable.
  1. Why is a 1-nearest-neighbour model on Tanimoto similarity a more meaningful baseline than the mean?
Because it is what a chemist does without a computer: find the closest known analogue and assume similar potency. Beating 1-NN shows the model has learned something beyond “similar molecules have similar activity” — here 1-NN reaches \(R^2\) = 0.243 against the forest’s 0.543.
  1. You standardise the full data matrix and then split. How bad is it, and how would you find out?
Usually mild, because scaling is unsupervised and a mean from 80% of the rows differs little from one over 100% — 382.03 against 381.59 g/mol here. You find out by running both protocols, as in Section 8.1. Avoid it anyway: the same habit applied to a supervised step is catastrophic.
  1. Which of these can safely be computed before the split: a Morgan fingerprint, a centring and scaling step, a PCA rotation, a molecular weight, a filter keeping bits present in more than 1% of compounds?
The fingerprint and the molecular weight — row-wise functions of one molecule. The scaler, the PCA and the frequency filter learn from the set as a whole and must be fitted inside the training fold; the filter in Section 3.4 kept a different number of bits (719 to 736) in each fold, which is the visible proof.
  1. Training RMSE 0.43, validation RMSE 0.74, validation curve still falling. What next?
Acquire more compounds: the curve has not plateaued. Reducing variance would also narrow the gap, but the slope says data is the cheapest remaining gain. Contrast Figure 6, where the curves converged at 1.04 and extra data is worthless.
  1. Your test \(R^2\) is slightly different from your cross-validated \(R^2\). Is something wrong?
No. A single test set of 553 compounds is one random draw; here the test RMSE is 0.738 against a cross-validated 0.742, a difference of 0.004 inside the fold-to-fold standard deviation of 0.027. The response is a confidence interval, not a comparison of two point estimates — Unit 12.
  1. Why does the model predict weak compounds as too potent and potent compounds as too weak?
Regression to the mean: minimising squared error against a bell-shaped target shrinks predictions towards the centre, most strongly where data are sparse. Absolute potency at the extremes is therefore unreliable while the ranking stays informative — Spearman \(\rho\) = 0.774 with \(R^2\) = 0.585.
  1. A feature called n_assays improves your model substantially. Should you keep it?
No. It is known only because the compound was tested, so it cannot be computed for a new molecule, and it correlates with potency because interesting compounds get re-tested. Same family as pActivity_min, which pushed \(R^2\) to 0.996.
  1. What does a negative cross-validated \(R^2\) mean?
That the model predicts held-out data worse than the training mean. It is the correct result for a model fitted to noise (−0.227 in Section 8.1) and common on small datasets; \(R^2\) is not bounded below by zero out of sample.
  1. How would you convert this regression into the ranking problem a screening campaign needs?
Keep the chain but evaluate with ranking metrics on the top slice: enrichment factor at 1%, BEDROC, Spearman \(\rho\) among the predicted top 100 (Unit 19). The change is in decisions 1, 6 and 7 — question, metric, error analysis — not in the algorithm.
  1. Your chain gives \(R^2\) = 0.93 where the literature reports 0.6. What do you do before celebrating?
Assume leakage and run the checklist: which feature columns could not be known before the target; duplicates straddling folds; selection or tuning that saw the validation folds; shuffled labels. Results far above the field’s norm are usually a bug.
  1. Why does the model card record performance separately for similar and dissimilar compounds?
Because the user is almost always asking about the dissimilar case. RMSE is 0.680 in the most-similar quartile and 0.802 in the least-similar; quoting only the pooled 0.738 overstates performance for the prospective use.

Glossary

Baseline
A deliberately simple predictor (the mean, the majority class, the nearest neighbour, a regularised linear model) whose score any real model must beat before it is worth discussing.
Censored measurement
A record stating only that a value lies above or below a bound (“IC50 > 10 µM”); usable as an inequality, not as a number.
Closure (R)
A function that returns another function together with the data it captured; the lightest way to express “fit once, apply many times” without a class system.
Descriptor
A single interpretable number computed from a structure (weight, lipophilicity, polar surface area, ring count…).
Error analysis
Study of which rows a model predicts worst and why; usually a ranked residual table annotated with domain information.
Learning curve
Training and validation error against training-set size; diagnoses underfitting (converged, high) versus overfitting (wide, persistent gap).
Leakage
Use at training or selection time of information unavailable at prediction time, including any use of the evaluation data to make a decision.
MAE / RMSE
Mean absolute error and root mean squared error; RMSE squares residuals and is dominated by the worst cases.
Model card
A short document stating what a model is, what it was trained and evaluated on, how it performs by subgroup, and where it must not be used.
Morgan fingerprint (ECFP)
A binary vector (here 2,048 bits) recording which circular atom environments a molecule contains; loaded in this edition from a frozen sparse file generated with RDKit.
pActivity
\(-\log_{10}\) of an activity concentration in molar; larger means more potent, one unit is tenfold.
Recipe (recipes)
A declarative list of preprocessing steps, estimated with prep() on training data and applied with bake(); the R counterpart of a column transformer.
R²
One minus residual over total sum of squares; relative to the variance of the evaluation set, and negative out of sample for a model worse than the mean.
Regression to the mean
The shrinkage of squared-error predictions towards the centre of the target distribution, seen as a tilt against the identity line.
Scaffold (Bemis–Murcko)
Ring systems plus linkers, side chains removed; a computable proxy for “chemical series”.
Tanimoto (Jaccard) similarity
Shared bits over union of bits between two fingerprints; the standard similarity for binary substructure vectors.
Unit of prediction
The entity one row represents and the model is asked to predict; must be the entity the question is about.
